Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infection has been linked to an increased risk of developing high blood pressure, or hypertension. This association is observed in various studies, particularly in populations where HCMV seropositivity rates are higher.

In the context of a nationally representative population-based survey from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), it was found that individuals with HCMV seropositivity were more likely to have hypertension. Specifically, women who tested positive for HCMV were also at an increased risk of developing hypertension.

The association between HCMV infection and hypertension is thought to be due in part to the effects of age on the development of both conditions. As people get older, their blood pressure tends to rise, while infections such as HCMV can cause chronic inflammation and changes in the cardiovascular system that may contribute to increased blood pressure.

While there are no definitive tests for detecting congenital cytomegalovirus infection in newborns, low birth weight and small head circumference at birth have been identified as predictors of congenital CMV infection. However, these factors do not directly predict hypertension.

Regarding the connection between sublingual varices and hypertension, research has shown that there is a link between the two conditions. Sublingual varices are enlarged veins in the neck that can be a symptom of internal bleeding due to high blood pressure. These varices have been found to increase the risk of developing hypertension.

The relationship between blood pressure measurement methods used by healthcare providers and those measured by patients may vary. Studies have shown that measurements taken by nurses tend to be lower than those taken by physicians for treated hypertensive patients, suggesting that this difference could contribute to a discrepancy in blood pressure readings.
